Experimental Mathematics
Pavel Snopov 1 * German Magai 2 *
Abstract

Recent advances in AI for Mathematics have focused largely on autoformalization and theorem proving, leaving the role of Computer Algebra Systems (CAS) in agentic LLM workflows underexplored. We propose a ReAct-style agentic setup that combines LLM reasoning with verifiable feedback from SageMath, together with Context7 for the up-to-date documentation. We evaluate this agentic setup across frontier models for solving research-level mathematical problems from the RealMath benchmark in a setting that emulates a computational-mathematics research loop. We also propose a refinement to the Real- Math benchmark by introducing a multi-step postprocessing procedure and a multi-stage validation pipeline, both of which improve the quality and reliability of the extracted problem set. Introduction

Recent progress in LLMs and agentic systems that integrate LLM reasoning with deterministic, verifiable tool backends such as compilers, theorem provers, SAT/SMT solvers, type checkers, and physical simulators has established a new neuro-symbolic paradigm in which generative reasoning is partially grounded in verifiable feedback. By coupling LLM reasoning with components that provide ground-truth signals, this paradigm enables a class of tools capable of automating tasks that previously required substantial expert effort and of producing answers with a level of reliability that purely generative approaches cannot achieve. A particularly active application of this paradigm is in mathematics. Substantial progress has been made on autoformalization, the translation of mathematical statements into the formal programs written in proof-assistant languages such as Lean, Coq, and Isabelle (Wu et al., 2022), as well as on automated theorem proving, where LLM-based systems guide the search for formal proofs (Lin et al., 2025), attain gold-medal-level performance on the 2025 International Mathematical Olympiad with formally verified solutions (Achim et al., 2025), and and have recently autonomously resolved several open problems from the Erd˝os collection (Sothanaphan, 2026; Tsoukalas et al., 2026) including the well-known unit-distance conjecture (OpenAI,

This workflow are common in computational and experimentally driven areas of mathematics. Despite the widespread use of CAS, their integration into LLM-based systems for mathematical reasoning has received substantially less attention than the integration of formal proof assistants. In particular, existing work has focused largely on formal proof construction, leaving computational workflows based on symbolic experimentation and executable verification comparatively underexplored. This gap, together with the recent successes of LLMs in mathematical reasoning, motivates the present study. The central question of our work is the following: to what extent does verifiable symbolic feedback improve the performance of frontier LLMs on research-level mathematics, and does it shape their behavior in agentic setup? To study this effect, we evaluate frontier LLMs within an agentic setup with an access to SageMath that closely emulates a mathematician’s computational workflow. The proposed setup is particularly relevant for tasks where symbolic computation plays a central role and where core mathematical structures have already been algorithmically formalized within existing software systems. Benchmarking AI4Math

Research-level benchmarks.A major line of benchmarks targets mathematics drawn from research-level tasks and literature rather than competitions. FRONTIERMATH(Glazer et al., 2024) pushes the difficulty ceiling with hundreds of unpublished problems crafted by leading mathematicians, including Terence Tao, spanning many research-adjacent areas. By mid-2026, the best reasoning LLMs reach over 50% on Tiers 1–3 and 25-40% on Tier 4 (Epoch AI, 2026). ETERNALMATH(Ma et al., 2026) pursues a fully automated theorem-grounded pipeline that turns recent papers into executable, verifiable tasks, with the goal of producing a continuously refreshable benchmark. An especially relevant work is REALMATH(Zhang et al., 2025), which proposes an automated data-collection pipeline that extracts research- 2

level problems from arXiv and Math Stack Exchange and presents them as (context, question, answer) triples, with a focus on constructive theorems. Our work builds on it, we use the computable subset of the dataset extracted by their pipeline, and also propose refinements to the benchmark. Tool-Augmented Agents for Mathematical

Discovery and Reasoning A complementary line of works combines agents with external symbolic and computational tools for the conjecturespace discovery and pruning in mathematical reasoning. FUNSEARCH(Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) and its successor ALPHAEVOLVE(Novikov et al., 2025) traverse the hypothesis space by evolving Python programs scored by a deterministic Python-based evaluator: FUNSEARCHproduced new lower bounds on the cap-set problem, and ALPHAE- VOLVEgeneralizes the loop to whole-codebase evolution and reports new SOTA constructions, including an improved scheme for 4×4 complex matrix multiplication. Early work in this direction includes (Chuharski et al., 2024), who sample conjectures about the solubilizer in group theory from LLMs and prune the conjecture space via counterexamples generated by GAP. The TORA (Gou et al., 2024) trains open-weight models to interleave reasoning with SymPy tool, substantially improving performance on competitionlevel benchmarks. MATHSENSEI(Das et al., 2024) combines a knowledge retriever, a Python program generator and executor, and the Wolfram-Alpha in a planner-driven pipeline, and ablates these tools on the MATH benchmark to isolate their complementary effects. We generalize this pattern to a general-purpose CAS-based tool and evaluate it on mathematical problem solving.
Experimental setup

We evaluate each model under two matched conditions: a tool-free baseline, in which the model solves each problem using direct reasoning alone, and a tool-augmented agentic setting, in which it can iteratively query SageMath and Context7. Apart from tool access and the corresponding system prompt, the base model and problem set are held fixed. This design isolates the effect of verifiable symbolic feedback on performance in research-level mathematics. We evaluate on a curated set of 133 problems from the RealMath benchmark and validate model outputs using a multi-stage protocol that combines symbolic equivalence checking with an LLM-as-a-judge stage. The system prompts for both pipelines are provided in Appendices F.1 and F.2.

blocks.text: The agentic pipeline is organized to emulate the workflow of a working mathematician. In the tool-free setting, the model relies on its internal knowledge resources and reasoning capabilities. However, the reasoning aimed to tackle a complicated mathematical problem might require intermediate computational steps with verifiable feedback. It would allow the agent to refine its reasoning through iterative experimentation and explore the hypothesis space more efficiently. We implement this pipeline by wrapping the models in a ReAct-style multi-turn loop, in which the agent repeatedly reasons about the current state, invokes an external tool, and incorporates the returned observation into the next turn. The tool interface provides access to SageMath for symbolic and computational mathematics and to Context7 for retrieving relevant library documentation. SageMath.SageMath (Sage) is a widely used opensource computer algebra system that provides a unified Python-based interface to a broad collection of mathematical software systems, including GAP, Singular, and PARI/GP. It supports symbolic computation, algebraic manipulation, and numerical experimentation, and provides extensive functionality for polynomial ideals, graph-theoretic computations, number theory, and related areas. In our pipeline, the agent can generate Sage code snippets, execute them in an isolated sandbox (see Appendix A.1), observe the returned output, and iterate on its hypotheses. blocks.text: Validating the equivalence of symbolic mathematical expressions is substantially more challenging than validating numerical answers, since structurally different expressions may still be mathematically equivalent. Prior benchmarks address this issue either through symbolic equivalence procedures (Shalyt et al., 2025) or through LLM-based judging (Tsoukalas et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). We combine both approaches in a multi-stage evaluation pipeline, as symbolic simplification is not exhaustive and may incorrectly reject mathematically equivalent expressions. Symbolic validator.The first stage compares the SymPyparsable output produced by the model against the groundtruth answer represented in the same format. Expressions are parsed into SymPy objects and their difference is simplified symbolically. If the resulting expression simplifies to zero, the prediction is considered correct. For multicomponent answers, outputs are compared component-wise. LLM-as-a-Judge validator.Cases rejected by the symbolic validator are not necessarily incorrect. For such cases, we employ a second-stage evaluation procedure based on three frontier LLM judges: Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3.5 Flash 3. Each model independently produces a verdict together with a short justification, and the final decision is obtained through majority voting. In addition, we manually inspect 30% of the cases reaching this stage and treat the resulting human annotations as ground truth. Evaluation metric.We report solve rate: the fraction of

blocks.text: Model efficiency on commonly solved problems.In practice, one often faces the choice of which model to deploy when a problem is relatively easy and the goal is to solve it at minimal cost. Here we therefore focus to the subset of problems solved by model within a given setup, accuracy is tied on this set by construction, so models are ranked purely by mean tokens per solved problem (Figure 4). Easiness is relative to the setup: the tool-augmented common set is larger (30 vs. 15 problems) and includes problems that only become universally solvable with CAS access. The two setups give opposite recommendations. Without tools, the cheapest configurations are open-weight: DeepSeek 3.2 (2.2k tokens), Qwen (2.3k), and DeepSeek V4-flash (2.6k). With tools, the top of the ranking is occupied entirely by closed models, GPT-5.5 ( 20k), Opus 4.7 ( 22k), and Opus 4.8 (29k) while the tool-free leaders drop to the bottom: DeepSeek-V3.2 falls to rank 11 ( 99k) and Qwen to rank 14 (131k). Therefore direct answering is thus not predictive of an efficient from the point of token usage agentic behavior. However, for relatively easy problems, a better strategy would be to first try an open-weight model such as DeepSeek before get expensive closed models. Finding 3.On easy problems solved by every model in the tool-free setup, the open-weight DeepSeek and Qwen models are the most token-efficient. blocks.text: Solve rate by mathematical category.We further examine the effect of the agentic setup on performance across arXiv categories (Figure 6). blocks.text: The present study has several limitations. First, the symbolic-verification procedure may fail to recognize correct answers, since robust universal equivalence checking remains difficult in the general case; the judge stage recovers 23–44% of credited solutions, so small inter-model gaps are methodologically fragile. Second, both dataset postprocessing and secondary validation rely on LLM outputs, which are not fully reliable. Third, the experimental dataset is limited in size and restricted to numerical or symbolicexpression answers that can be normalized and automatically checked, introducing selection bias toward the computationally executable subset of research-level mathematics. Finally, the tool-augmented setting combines SageMath, Context7, ReAct prompting, and a tool-use budget; thus, gains cannot be attributed to CAS access alone.

blocks.text: Tool-Assisted Iterative Computation

In this section, we examine in detail a solution trajectory for a representative problem, illustrating how a CAS-augmented GPT-5.5 can exhibit key elements of a computational mathematician’s workflow. Rather than querying SageMath for the target invariants directly, the agent iteratively formulates and tests conjectures, diagnoses errors, and extracts patterns from computational results. Neither invariant is directly implemented as a SageMath routine, requiring the agent to infer the target formulas indirectly based on iterative computation. The problem is drawn from (Himeno & Teragaito, 2024) and focuses on the torsion order Ord(K) and the second torsion order Ord′(K) of the twisted torus knot K= T(p, kp+ 1; 2,1). Specifically, the task asks for closedform expressions for Ord(K) when p≥2 and for Ord′(K) when p≥4 . . Summary.This example illustrates a successful form of tool-augmented mathematical reasoning. SageMath was not used as an oracle for Ord(K) or Ord′(K), since neither invariant was directly implemented. Instead, the agent used SageMath to compute accessible intermediate objects: braid Alexander polynomials, exponent gaps, and Smith normal forms over F2[U]. It recovered from an implementation error caused by Sage’s exponent representation, converted Alexander polynomial data into staircase lengths, and used Smith invariant factors to detectU-torsion exponents. The resulting formulas were not returned by a single Sage command, but were obtained through an iterative process in which the agent computed examples, identified patterns, formulated conjectures, and validated them across other parameters. In this sense, the agent’s approach resembles a computational experiment: SageMath supplied evidences, while the agent used its mathematical knowledge to interpret it and infer the conjectural closed forms.
Conclusions

We evaluated 15 frontier LLMs on 133 research-level mathematical problems derived from the RealMath benchmark, comparing direct-answer inference against a ReAct-style agentic pipeline equipped with SageMath and Context7 documentation retrieval. Tool access improved the solve rate of every evaluated model, by +9.7 pp on average, with gains ranging from +1.5 pp (Kimi K2.7) to +27.8 pp (Qwen 3.7- Max, improving from 42.1% to 69.9%). OpenAI’s flagship model, GPT-5.5, achieved the highest solve rate of75.2% at the lowest token usage among tool-enabled configurations, dominating every other model on both axes; it is followed by Opus 4.8 (73.7%) and the multi-agent orchestration system Fugu-Ultra, which matches Opus 4.7 at 72.9% while being the second most token-efficient configuration. The CAS access substantially narrowed the gap between open-weight and closed frontier models. 12

Beyond overall solve rates, our experiments reveal consistent behavioral patterns that separate effective and ineffective tool-augmented agents. Gains are non-uniform: openweight models improve more than twice as much as closed models on average, largely due to weaker tool-free baselines, yet higher token expenditure does not translate into higher accuracy, and the token-efficiency ranking inverts between setups: open-weight models consume the fewest tokens at direct answering but the most as agents. Agentic runs are strongly bimodal: strong models solve a problem within the first 3–4 tool interactions, using SageMath mainly to verify solutions already derived through reasoning, whereas weaker agents exhaust the entire tool budget searching for a solution through computation, writing long-running code. Consistently, recovery dynamics after failed tool calls vary far more across models than raw failure rates, constituting a axis separating effective and ineffective agents. More broadly, our results support the view that computer algebra systems provide a promising substrate for computational and experimental mathematics with LLM agents. Our case study shows that a CAS-augmented agent can reproduce key elements of a working mathematician’s workflow: computing accessible intermediate objects, extracting patterns from examples, formulating conjectures, and validating them across parameters. While current systems remain limited on problems requiring deep theoretical insight or specialized contemporary knowledge, the observed gains

indicate that executable symbolic computation can substantially extend the practical reasoning capabilities of frontier models, and we view this direction as a step toward automated mathematical experimentation and computational conjecture discovery. As future work, we propose a multiagent architecture that assigns distinct responsibilities to agents equipped with a diverse set of tools.
Impact Statement

This work studies CAS-assisted LLM agents for research mathematics. It advances verifiable AI-assisted scientific reasoning; we foresee no specific societal risks beyond those already recognized and release our evaluation set and validation pipeline for reproducibility.

blocks.text: A. Experimental Details
A.1. Implementation Details

SageMath Sandbox.All SageMath execution is performed in an ephemeral Docker container. For each tool call, a generated Sage program is launched through a small wrapper. This wrapper imports sage.all, runs Sage’s preparser to standardize Sage syntax, executes the script and extracts the designated result variable. It also captures standard output and returns a JSON-friendly representation of the result to the host. For each tool call, the generated code snippet is executed in a fresh interpreter. The execution is limited to 2 CPU cores, 4 GB of memory, a 45s wall-clock timeout, and a 50s CPU-time limit. The executed code has no network access. The host also rejects outputs larger than 262,144 bytes before parsing the returned result to prevent excessively large intermediate outputs. Failure handling is normalized into a small number of categories. User-code exceptions are returned as code error together with the captured traceback. Docker startup failures, such as an unavailable daemon or missing image, are classified as docker error. Container crashes or abnormal exits are classified as runtime crash, and wall-clock overruns are classified astimeout; in the timeout case the host forcibly removes the container.
A.2. Dataset Construction

We begin with the dataset of 633 problems obtained from the RealMath benchmark (Zhang et al., 2025). We focus on this dataset because it is derived from the contemporary mathematical literature. Each problem from this dataset contains the question, context and the answer, each of which is represented in a LaTeX format. We also enrich the dataset enriching it with the arXiv categories that were associated with the papers from which the corresponding problems were scraped via the RealMath extraction pipeline. If the paper had several categories, only the first one was used. We automatically retain only those tasks whose final answers can be normalized into executable SymPy (Meurer et al.,

Model-specific observations GPT-5.5.The dominant configuration: tools lift its solve rate from 67.7% to 75.2%, the best result overall, at the lowest cost (34k tokens and 3.8 Sage calls per problem, median trace of 1). It combines an 85% call-success rate with the best post-failure recovery (77%), self-finalizes 91% of runs, and contributes the largest single-model coverage (100/133) to the ensemble analysis. Opus 4.8.The second-best solve rate overall ( 73.7%, up from 66.2% without tools), reached with a compact agentic tool call traces (3.6 calls per problem, median trace of 2, 89% self-finalization). Its one weakness is timeouts: 22.6% of its Sage calls exceed the wall-clock limit, the highest share among the 4 leading models, which decreases its raw call-success rate (66%) without noticeably hurting its accuracy. Opus 4.7.Tool access improves solve rate from 61.7% to 72.9%, 16 problems gained. It has the cleanest tool-interaction profile in the study: the fewest Sage calls overall (435; 3.3 per problem), an 84% call-success rate, zero NameErrors, 92% self-finalization, and the shortest sandbox time per problem (29s). Fugu-Ultra.Tied with Gemini 3.1 Pro for the second-strongest tool-free baseline ( 66.9%, behind GPT-5.5). Fugu-Ultra reaches 72.9% with tools: short, clean code (median 662 characters), an 85% call-success rate, and no interpreter-state errors. Its token multiplier under tool access is the smallest of any model (4.5×, 70k tokens per problem), placing it second on the accuracy-cost plane among frontier models after GPT-5.5.

blocks.text: E. Case Studies

This section presents case studies of six representative problems that were solved correctly by LLM agents with SageMath access. Each problem is described in a separate subsection, which provides the problem statement and final answer. Additionally we briefly summarize the agent’s solution strategy based on an analysis of the tool-call traces logged during the experimental runs. In the final we provide two examples of problems that required the highest number of tokens for a tool-free zero-shot run among problems solved by only one model.
